title: Contractor Ghosted Me During House Flip: What to Do Right Now
excerpt: Getting ghosted by a contractor mid-flip can derail your entire deal and cost you thousands. Here's exactly what to do when a contractor disappears and how to protect yourself going forward.
author: AIWholesail Team
tags: contractor ghosted me during house flip what to do
metaDescription: Contractor ghosted you during a house flip? Follow these step-by-step actions to recover your project, protect your money, and finish the flip profitably.

sections.content: You handed over a $15,000 deposit, the demo crew came through, and then... silence. Calls go to voicemail. Texts get three grey checkmarks. Your contractor has vanished, and your half-gutted property is sitting there bleeding holding costs every single day. If you're asking yourself 'my contractor ghosted me during my house flip — what do I do?', you are not alone. This happens more than most investors admit, and the investors who recover fastest are the ones who move quickly and methodically.
Why Contractors Ghost Mid-Project

Before you take action, it helps to understand what is actually happening. Contractors ghost for a handful of predictable reasons. They took on too many jobs at once and overcommitted. They ran out of money — sometimes your deposit funded another project that went sideways. They hit a scope problem they do not know how to solve. Or, in the worst cases, they were never qualified to begin with. Understanding the 'why' helps you decide how hard to push for your money back versus how fast to simply replace them and move on.
Step 1: Document Everything Immediately

The moment you realize your contractor has gone quiet, start building a paper trail. Time-stamp everything. Screenshot your last text exchange, save voicemail recordings, and take dated photos of the current state of the property. Note exactly what work was completed versus what was paid for. This documentation is essential whether you pursue a contractor's bond claim, small claims court, or just need leverage to negotiate a partial refund. Investors in active markets like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga) and [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx) deal with this issue regularly, and local attorneys consistently say documentation is the single biggest factor in winning disputes.

Take a full video walkthrough of the property within 24 hours of realizing your contractor has disappeared. Walk every room, narrate what is done versus incomplete, and note any materials left on-site. Upload it to cloud storage immediately so it is time-stamped and preserved.
Step 2: Send a Formal Written Notice

Send a certified letter — not just a text — to the contractor's address of record. State clearly that they are in breach of contract, specify the work that was not completed, and give them a firm deadline of 3 to 5 business days to respond. This written notice does two things: it creates a legal record, and it sometimes shakes a contractor loose who thought they could just avoid the situation. Keep your tone professional. You want leverage, not a screaming match that makes you look unreasonable if this ends up in front of a judge or licensing board.
Step 3: File a Complaint and Explore Recovery Options
Contractor Licensing Board

Every state has a contractor licensing board, and filing a complaint is free. Licensed contractors risk losing their license if a complaint is sustained. This is often your most powerful lever because it threatens their livelihood. Check whether your contractor is actually licensed — you may discover they were operating without one, which opens up additional legal options.
Surety Bond Claims

Many licensed contractors are required to carry a surety bond. If your contractor abandoned the project, you may be able to file a bond claim directly with their bonding company. Bond claims can recover money for unfinished work or deposits paid on work never started. The bonding company will investigate and, if the claim is valid, pay you up to the bond amount — often $10,000 to $25,000 depending on the state and license class.
Small Claims and Civil Court

Small claims court handles disputes up to $10,000 in most states, and you do not need a lawyer. For larger amounts, a real estate attorney can send a demand letter — sometimes that alone is enough to prompt a settlement. If the contractor has assets, a civil judgment can be collected against bank accounts or equipment.
Step 4: Get Your Numbers Right Before Hiring Anyone New

Before you bring in a replacement contractor, you need to know exactly where you stand financially. Pull out your original scope of work and mark off what was completed, what was half-done, and what was never touched. Then get fresh bids — minimum three — on the remaining work. Rehab costs often creep up after a contractor swap because new crews charge more to take on someone else's mess. Be realistic about your revised budget and recalculate your profit margin before committing to finish. Use the free [Rehab Estimator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/rehab-estimator) to quickly reprice the remaining scope and see whether your deal still makes sense before you pour more money in.
The second contractor always costs more than the first quote. Budget for a 15 to 20 percent premium when you bring in a replacement mid-project — then be pleasantly surprised if it comes in lower.
Step 5: Vet Your Replacement Contractor Harder This Time

items: Verify their license and insurance directly with your state licensing board — do not just take their word for it
Call at least three recent references and ask specifically about project completion and communication
Never pay more than 10 to 15 percent as an upfront deposit — tie remaining payments to completed milestones
Get a detailed written contract with a completion timeline and a penalty clause for delays
Visit other active job sites they are running before signing anything
Add a 'right to cure' clause so you can hire a third party if they fall behind and bill the difference back to them

sections.content: Step 6: Manage Your Holding Costs Aggressively

Every day your flip sits idle is money leaving your pocket. A typical hard money loan runs 10 to 14 percent annually, which works out to roughly $50 to $90 per day on a $150,000 loan. Add property taxes, insurance, and utilities and a two-month contractor delay can easily eat $8,000 to $12,000 in holding costs alone. In competitive markets like [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), where values can shift quarter to quarter, a stalled project also risks market timing problems. Move quickly on finding a replacement and consider offering a small completion bonus to incentivize speed.

Ask your replacement contractor if they can start with a crew already in place rather than scheduling weeks out. Offering 5 to 10 percent above their standard rate for a fast start is often cheaper than two more months of holding costs.
How to Protect Yourself on Every Future Flip

The best way to handle a ghosting contractor is to never be in a vulnerable position when it happens. Structure every contract so you are never significantly overpaid versus work completed. Use a draw schedule tied to inspections: rough-in payment after rough-in inspection passes, trim payment after trim is installed, and so on. Keep a 10 percent retainer until the punch list is fully signed off. Investors who follow this model rarely lose serious money when a contractor disappears because they have not paid for work that was not done yet.
